description: We're a curious crew who can't stop looking up. Some of us think in code, some in equations, some in stars, and we all love asking "what if?" We mix science, creativity, and a lot of late night ideas to build things that bring space a little closer to everyone here on Earth.
summary:
What if the landscapes of Mars and the Moon weren’t as different from Earth as we imagine? That question inspired Space Twins, an interactive website that brings planetary exploration a little closer to home.

Using scientific data from NASA, we created a space where anyone can explore fascinating locations on Mars and the Moon, discover their geological features, and find similar places on Earth. Through our “Find Your Space Twin” tool, users can compare landscapes based on terrain, minerals, and surface conditions, with results expressed as similarity percentages.

But Space Twins is more than a comparison tool. It combines science, interactive exploration, and educational games to make learning about other worlds feel exciting and accessible. Our goal is to spark curiosity, encourage scientific thinking, and show how studying Earth’s landscapes can offer valuable insights for future space exploration.

Because sometimes, discovering another world begins with looking at our own.
details:
Space Twins is an interactive website where you can explore different places on Mars and the Moon and compare them with similar locations on Earth. Using scientific data from NASA, we wanted to show how these worlds can share geological and environmental features.

When you open the website, you’ll see Mars and the Moon rotating on the screen. By clicking on Mars, you can explore places like Jezero Crater, Oxia Planum, Valles Marineris, and Arcadia Planitia. Each location includes images, short descriptions, and information about its geological features. You can also explore specific areas, like lowland plains or highland terrain, to learn more about their rocks, minerals, and surface conditions.

On the Moon, you can visit places like Shackleton Crater, Mons Mouton, the Lunar South Pole, the South Pole–Aitken Basin, Oceanus Procellarum, and Mare Serenitatis. Just like on Mars, you can explore different types of terrain, including upper plateaus, scarp edges, and nearby craters.

One of our main features is “Find Your Space Twin,” which helps you discover places on Earth that share similarities with the regions you’re exploring. You can choose between robotic exploration, geological research, or resource prospecting. The website then calculates a similarity percentage based on factors like slope, surface roughness, and materials, and explains how the result was calculated.

We also added a game where users can look at two landscapes and guess how similar they are. There’s also an option to suggest new locations on Earth by adding coordinates, descriptions, and geological information. These suggestions go through an evaluation process before being added. The About section explains the comparison methods, scientific criteria, and limitations of the system.

To build Space Twins, we used Cloud, ChatGPT, and HTML to develop the website, organize scientific information, and work on its interactive features. Throughout the process, we focused on reliable data, terrain differences, easy navigation, and making the results clear and understandable.

What makes Space Twins different is that it doesn’t just show information about other worlds. It lets you connect them with real places on Earth through scientific comparisons and interactive activities.

Our goal is to make space exploration easier to understand and more enjoyable, especially for students and anyone curious about science. We also want to show how these comparisons can help us better understand other planets and support future geological research, robotic exploration, and space missions.
